name: Sultanate of Ifat
info: A Sunni Muslim sultanate of the Walashma dynasty in eastern Shewa, reaching from Zequalla to the port of Zeila, that fought Ethiopia's Christian emperors from 1320 until its defeat on the Harar plateau in 1403.

facts.capital: Ifat (Wafāt), probably at Walalah in eastern Shewa; the Harar plateau and Zeila under Haqq ad-Din II
facts.founder: Umar ibn Dunya-huz, Sultan Umar Walasma, founder of the Walashma dynasty, who died around 1275
facts.predecessor: Sultanate of Shewa, conquered by Umar Walasma; the Muslim states of Gidaya, Dawaro, Bale and Fatagar
facts.successor: Adal Sultanate, with its capital at Harar; the Ethiopian Empire's provinces of Yifat and Menz

t: Ibn Sa'id al-Maghribi placed the capital Wafāt on high ground in a river valley where the people grew bananas and sugar cane; al-Umari counted seven cities, an army of 20,000 soldiers and 15,000 horsemen, and a ruler who wore headbands of silk.

Sabr ad-Din's rebellion of 1332 aimed to make him king of all Ethiopia, turn the churches into mosques and set the Christian queen to grind corn; Emperor Amda Seyon destroyed Ifat's capital, looted his camp of gold and slaves, imprisoned him and installed his brother Jamal ad-Din I.

Haqq ad-Din II moved the capital to the Harar plateau and fought the emperor in more than twenty battles before dying in 1376; his brother Sa'ad ad-Din II was defeated in 1403 and killed at Zeila, after which, al-Maqrizi wrote, 'the strength of the Muslims was abated'.
dyk: When Emperor Amda Seyon threatened in 1320 to divert the Nile and starve Egypt unless the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad stopped persecuting the Copts, the Egyptians dismissed it as an idle threat; the fear that Ethiopia might tamper with the Nile nonetheless stayed with them for centuries.
ev: Sultan Umar Walasma, founder of the dynasty, dies after carving out his kingdom and conquering the Sultanate of Shewa; 'four or five sons' rule briefly before Sabr ad-Din I.
Sultan Wali Asma imposes his rule on Hubat, Zeila and the other Muslim states of the region.
Haqq ad-Din I invades Amhara, burns churches, forces conversions and kills the emperor's envoy; Amda Seyon I raids Shewa and Ifat, and Dadader Haqq ad-Din falls at the battle of Marra Biete.
Sabr ad-Din rebels to become 'King of all Ethiopia'; Amda Seyon destroys the capital of Ifat, imprisons him and appoints Jamal ad-Din I in his place.
Haqq ad-Din II, who moved the capital to the Harar plateau and fought over twenty battles with the emperor, dies in battle; his brother Sa'ad ad-Din II succeeds.
Ifat's troops are defeated on the Harar plateau; Sa'ad ad-Din II flees to Zeila and is killed there, by al-Maqrizi's account (another source dates his death to 1410 under Emperor Yeshaq).

sections.foundation:
Islam came to the Horn of Africa from Arabia soon after the hijra. Zeila's two-mihrab mosque, the Masjid al-Qiblatayn, dates from about the seventh century and is among the oldest in Africa; in the late ninth century al-Yaqubi described Muslims living along the northern Somali seaboard and Zeila as a self-governing trading port whose merchants shipped goods to Yemen and Egypt. Inland, the Sultanate of Shewa is believed to have been the first Muslim state of the interior; by its chronicle the conversion of its people began in 1108 with the Gbbah.

The Walashma dynasty founded Ifat. Umar ibn Dunya-huz, later known as Sultan Umar Walasma, carved out a kingdom of his own and conquered the Sultanate of Shewa; in 1288 Sultan Wali Asma imposed his rule on Hubat, Zeila and the other Muslim states of the region, a consolidation of the Muslim lands that Taddesse Tamrat compares with Emperor Yekuno Amlak's consolidation of the Christian highlands in the same years. The dynasty claimed Arab descent from the Hejaz and the Quraysh through Aqil ibn Abi Talib, a lineage most probably invented for prestige: the Walashma were most likely of local origin. By al-Maqrizi's account Umar died around 1275 and 'four or five sons' ruled briefly until Sabr ad-Din I held power to the turn of the century; his successor Sultan Ali was the first to war with Abyssinia and soon submitted again for want of popular support.
sections.socioeconomy:
The earliest account of Ifat is Ibn Sa'id al-Maghribi's: the region was called Jabarta and its capital Wafāt, a city on high ground in a valley beside a river, on the eastern edge of Shewa, whose Muslim inhabitants of mixed descent grew bananas and sugar cane. Al-Umari placed the state near the Red Sea coast, fifteen days' travel by twenty, with a river (the Awash) and a large population, and named seven cities, Biqulzar, Kwelgora, Shimi, Shewa, Adal, Jamme and Laboo. His account implies a land 300 by 400 kilometres, which Richard Pankhurst thinks exaggerated. Five ruined towns of the fourteenth century, Asbäri, Nora, Mäsal, Rassa Guba and Beri-Ifat, have been found in eastern Shewa, their houses resembling Argobba and Harari building.

Wealth came through Zeila. The port, near the Bab al-Mandab strait, was a node of transcontinental trade and the most important entry point for Islam into the Ethiopian lands, and Ifat's rulers controlled it as a commercial and religious base. The people were diverse: nomadic Somalis, Afars and Warjih, already Muslim by the thirteenth century, the Silte, Hararis and Argobbas, and the now extinct Doba and Harla. Arabic was the lingua franca, but the inhabitants spoke Cushitic and Ethio-Semitic languages. Khat, forbidden to Orthodox Christians, was widely chewed by Muslims at Mar'ade, and the ruler of Ifat wore headbands of silk.
sections.military:
Al-Umari credited Ifat with an army of 20,000 soldiers and 15,000 horsemen; its infantry, according to Mohammed Hassen, were the Argobba. Its wars were with the Christian empire. In 1320 Haqq ad-Din I invaded the Amhara kingdom, burnt churches, forced Christians to apostatise, seized the emperor's envoy on his way back from Cairo and killed him when he would not convert; the emperor raided all Shewa, then largely Muslim, and the districts of Ifat. His son Dadader Haqq ad-Din fell at the battle of Marra Biete. In early 1332 Sabr ad-Din divided his troops in three, sending one division against Amhara, one against Angot and leading the third into Shewa.

Amda Seyon paid his soldiers in gold, silver and fine clothes, yet many would not march into Ifat's arid, roadless mountains; those who did advanced on 24 Yakatit, put the sultan to flight, destroyed his capital, killed many of his soldiers and sacked a camp, taking its people as slaves. Sabr ad-Din surrendered and was imprisoned. Haqq ad-Din II fought the emperor ceaselessly from the Harar plateau and Zeila, in more than twenty battles to 1370, and died in battle in 1376; Sa'ad ad-Din II waged hit-and-run raids and struck chiefs loyal to the emperor at Zalan and Hadeya, until the imperial army defeated Ifat on the Harar plateau in 1403. A court hymn for Emperor Yishaq's victory over the sultan's troops holds the first known mention of the name Somali.
sections.governance:
Ifat was ruled by the Walashma sultans from their capital in eastern Shewa, and later from the Harar plateau and Zeila. The states of eastern Ethiopia that had preceded it, Gidaya, Dawaro, Sawans, Bali and Fatagar, were incorporated into the sultanate but kept a measure of independence; Taddesse Tamrat counts Fatagar, Dawaro and Bale within its borders, and Fatagar stayed under Ifat's control after the rest were invaded. Ifat kept its own diplomacy: it sent an embassy under Shaykh Abdallah al-Zayla'i to the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad in Cairo.

After 1332 the sultans were vassals of the Christian emperor, who claimed the right to make them. Amda Seyon imprisoned Sabr ad-Din and appointed his brother Jamal ad-Din I; his son Sayfa Arad named Ahmad, Harb Arad ibn Ali, sultan and jailed Ali's father and relatives, but Ahmad was killed in an Ifat uprising and his son Haqq ad-Din II won the throne through a series of battles against his kinsman Mola Asfah. Tegulat, once the capital of the Shewa sultanate and known to Muslims as Mar'ade, became Amda Seyon's own seat, and the emperor appointed the Walasma descendants king of all the Muslim lands. Islam governed the state: the chroniclers of Amda Seyon treat Sabr ad-Din's war, with its governors appointed for Fatagar, Alamalé, Damot, Amhara, Angot, Inderta, Begemder and Gojjam and its threat to plant khat at the capital, as a jihad rather than a bid for independence.
sections.impact:
Ifat was the northernmost of the Muslim states of the Horn and the buffer between the Christian kingdom and the Muslim states of the coast. Through Zeila it was the most important entry point for Islam into the Ethiopian lands, and under its rule the faith spread: by the middle of the fourteenth century the Muslim peoples north of the Awash were under the sultanate. Its wars were also part of a wider contest. Mordechai Abir ties them to the conflict between Egypt and Ethiopia: the Mamluks' persecution of the Copts provoked Amda Seyon's threats in 1320, the arrest of Patriarch Marcos in 1352 led Ethiopia to imprison every Egyptian merchant, and only in 1361 did Sultan al-Malik al-Salih free the patriarch and seek friendship with the emperor.

The sultanate's fall shaped the region's next two centuries. Haqq ad-Din II's removal of the capital to the Harar plateau makes him for some the true founder of the Adal Sultanate, which emerged with Harar as its capital as the leading Muslim principality of the south-east in the later fifteenth century. By Harari tradition the Argobba fled Ifat for the Aw Abdal lowlands around Harar during the fifteenth-century war. Smaller territories went on being ruled by Walasma groups until the eighteenth century, when Christian dynasties named Yifat and Menz, after the sultanate's provinces, arose in their place; the name survives in the Ethiopian district of Yifat in North Shewa of the Amhara region.
sections.decline:
Sa'ad ad-Din II, who succeeded his brother in 1376, kept up the attacks on the Abyssinian Christian army and on the chiefs who supported the emperor at Zalan and Hadeya in hit-and-run raids. Early in the fifteenth century the emperor, probably Dawit I, gathered a large army, branded the Muslims of the region 'enemies of the Lord' and invaded. After much fighting Ifat's troops were defeated on the Harar plateau in 1403, and the sultan fled to Zeila with Ethiopian soldiers in pursuit. Al-Maqrizi relates that the Amhara besieged him on the peninsula of Zeila, cut off his water, were shown a way to him 'by one of the impious', and after three days of battle wounded him in the forehead and pierced him with their swords, so that 'he died happily, falling in God's cause'.

No other contemporary source confirms the invasion of Zeila, and an Amhara incursion there is thought unlikely; another contemporary source dates Sa'ad ad-Din's death to 1410 and credits Emperor Yeshaq with killing him. After his death, al-Maqrizi wrote, 'the strength of the Muslims was abated', the Amhara settled the country and made churches of the ravaged mosques, and the followers of Islam were harassed for more than twenty years. The Walashma survived in Adal, whose capital Harar led the Muslims of the south-east from the later fifteenth century.

summary: The Sultanate of Ifat, ruled by the Walashma from eastern Shewa to the port of Zeila, consolidated the Muslim lands of the Horn in the late thirteenth century and fought the Christian emperors from 1320. Crushed by Amda Seyon in 1332 and defeated on the Harar plateau in 1403, it gave way to the Adal Sultanate at Harar.
references: Taddesse Tamrat, Church and State in Ethiopia, 1270–1527 (Clarendon Press, 1972)
J. Spencer Trimingham, Islam in Ethiopia (Oxford University Press, 1952)

pointDescs.1285: The Walashma dynasty rules Ifat after Umar Walasma's conquest of the Sultanate of Shewa; by al-Maqrizi's account Umar died around 1275 and his sons rule in turn.
pointDescs.1288: Sultan Wali Asma imposes his rule on Hubat, Zeila and the other Muslim states of the region, consolidating the Muslim lands of the Horn.
pointDescs.1300: Sabr ad-Din I rules Ifat to the turn of the century; his successor Sultan Ali is the first to make war on Abyssinia and soon submits again.
pointDescs.1320: Ifat at its height, as al-Umari describes it: seven cities, 20,000 soldiers and 15,000 horsemen; Haqq ad-Din I invades Amhara and the war with Amda Seyon I begins.
pointDescs.1332: Sabr ad-Din's rebellion to become king of all Ethiopia ends with the destruction of Ifat's capital, his imprisonment and the installation of Jamal ad-Din I as the emperor's man.
pointDescs.1350: By the middle of the fourteenth century the Muslim peoples north of the Awash and much of Ankober are under the sultanate; Egypt's arrest of Patriarch Marcos in 1352 renews the wider conflict.
pointDescs.1370: Haqq ad-Din II, ruling from the Harar plateau and Zeila, has fought the emperor in more than twenty battles by this year.
pointDescs.1376: Haqq ad-Din II dies in battle; his brother Sa'ad ad-Din II succeeds and continues the attacks on the Christian army and its allied chiefs.
pointDescs.1403: Ifat's troops are defeated on the Harar plateau and Sa'ad ad-Din II is killed at Zeila, by al-Maqrizi's account; 'the strength of the Muslims was abated'.
pointDescs.1415: The Amhara settle the country, turn ravaged mosques into churches and harass the Muslims for over twenty years; another source dates the sultan's death to 1410 under Yeshaq. Adal rises at Harar.

notes: Register dates 1285–1415 against the article: Umar Walasma died c. 1275 (so the dynasty predates 1285), Wali Asma's consolidation is 1288, and the end is 1403 (al-Maqrizi, Dawit I) or 1410 (another source, Yeshaq). The first point keeps 1285 and the last 1415, with descriptions that give the article's dates.

The article is inconsistent on the founder's name (Umar ibn Dunya-huz / Umar Walasma / 'Sultan Wali Asma' in 1288) and on the first ruler to fight Abyssinia (Sultan Ali under Yagbe'u Seyon, then 'the conflict began' in 1320 under Haqq ad-Din I); both are kept as the article gives them.
The 1350 point rests on the article's 'by the mid-fourteenth century' spread of Islam and the 1352 arrest of Patriarch Marcos; 1370 on 'over twenty battles through 1370'.
The phrase 'in God's cause' is al-Maqrizi's, quoted only where he uses it, of Sa'ad ad-Din's death.
The military section's claim that the Argobba were Ifat's infantry is attributed to Mohammed Hassen, as in the article; the Somali hymn is placed under Yishaq (Yeshaq) as the article spells it there.
No references: the article's reference list is empty; the scholars it names (Taddesse Tamrat, Pankhurst, Huntingford, Abir, Trimingham, Levtzion and Pouwels, Braukämper) appear without titles.
